projects.title: CAD Saab JAS 39 Gripen Fighter Jet
projects.description: Created a detailed CAD model of the Saab JAS 39 Gripen in SolidWorks using complex 3D sketches, loft features, and advanced mating techniques. Applied realistic appearances, decals, and color schemes to replicate the visual profile of the Swedish fighter aircraft. Conducted a linear static FEA to simulate aerodynamic lift on the wings, evaluating structural response under upward force conditions.

projects.title: MATLAB Asymmetrical Bending Analysis Tool
projects.description: ● Developed a MATLAB suite to model stress distributions in femur cross-sections under asymmetrical bending with and without implants● Computed stress distributions, neutral axis orientation, and centroid locations using BMD-weighted Young’s modulus maps derived from medical image data● Evaluated stress normalization metrics and visualized results via custom contour plots

projects.title: 3D Printed Wind Turbine Design and Testing
projects.description: Designed and tested a 3D-printed wind turbine to optimize power output, structural stability, and weight efficiency. Developed a rotor blade and generator housing within strict design constraints, achieving a peak power output of 0.8041 W and a tower stiffness of 18.0 N/m (evaluated through linear regression analysis of applied load vs. displacement). Applied iterative CAD modeling and performance testing, ensuring compliance with project guidelines while refining key engineering metrics.

projects.title: Night Phone Holder – Adjustable Rotating Stand
projects.description: ● Developed a phone clamp system with upper and lower jaws, dual railings, and adjustable arms for a secure fit● Engineered ball and socket joints for rotational flexibility, incorporating knurled surfaces and sticky coatings to enhance grip● Manufactured components using resin for durability and flexibility, preventing breakage compared to PLA alternatives● Designed a base clamp with interference fit, ensuring stability on various surfaces● Drafted fully dimensioned detail and assembly drawings with Geometric Dimensioning & Tolerancing (GD&T), applying tolerances using ANSI B4.1 Standard Limits and Fits to ensure intended function● Conducted performance testing, refining the design for ease of use and accessibility

projects.title: LEAPFROG
projects.description: As a member of Space Technologies at California, I led the development of a custom testing rig for our hopper system. The compression phase of the hopper is constrained by the bending strength of carbon fiber rods, allowing a maximum vertical contraction of 40% before risking fracture.Each carbon fiber rod experiences approximately 10N of force in a short burst, generating a high impulse that enables substantial propulsion despite the hopper’s small size. I also assisted in refining the compression-based jumping mechanism, utilizing carbon fiber rods to achieve a projected jump height of 14 meters on the moon.

activity.title: Two all-nighters. No Wi-Fi. And the first prototype of KitchenOS was born. Last weekend, I built the first prototype of KitchenOS during Cal Hacks , the world’s largest hackathon. Our vision: reinvent food automation. With no internet connection for two days, we had to improvise and optimize locally — fine-tuning the ACT Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model to control a robotic arm with precision. We relied on LeRobot, a Hugging Face framework for embodied AI, and pushed it to its limits. Two all-nighters, three hours of sleep, and one dream taking shape. This is just the first step for KitchenOS , a project I’ll be developing all year long. Massive thanks to my incredible teammates Princess Tayab , Bhavya Mamnani , Zahra Mokhtari and to the mentors Théo Michel , David Dobas , George K. , and Alan Helmick who helped me navigate such a complex technical roadmap. If you’re passionate about robotics, food automation, or embodied AI — or if you’re an investor interested in the future of kitchens — feel free to reach out. This journey is just beginning, and it’s going to be wild :) 🚀🍔

Second place at my first ever hackathon 🤗 Last weekend, I had the amazing experience of taking part in the world's largest collegiate hackathon, Cal Hacks , in San Francisco! Jaansi Parsa , Julia Mathew , Bhavya Mamnani , and I created Peps Towards Sustainability, an interactive web app that visualizes how effectively PepsiCo 's numerous sustainability initiatives are contributing to its 2030 ESG goals. Using data from published reports and linear regression models, we classify whether the company is on track to meet key benchmarks in agriculture, packaging, water, transportation, etc., and summarize their overall performance using a unified metric. We ended up winning UC Berkeley Sutardja Center for Entrepreneurship and Technology (SCET) and PepsiCo 's PEP+ Sustainability Prize! I feel incredibly grateful to have gotten the opportunity to meet all the other passionate hackers at the competition and be inspired by their projects. Excited for more to come!!!

A year ago, I had no idea what a hackathon even entailed. So, when Andrea Li , Julia Mathew , Bhavya Mamnani , and I decided to form a team for Cal Hacks 11.0, our first ever hackathon, we never could have imagined that we would walk away with a second place award in the Pepsico Sustainability Prize! Inspired by Pepsico’s vast global operations and commitment to sustainability, we sought to create a centralized system to assess their sustainability efforts. We developed an interactive web app that creates a unified metric to measure the company's sustainability performance across agriculture, packaging, water, and transportation. It quantifies Pepsi's environmental impact, then predicts future progress and calculates their deviation from optimal sustainability targets. More than anything, I'm really grateful for how much I learned at Cal Hacks, both from people and experiences. This was such an amazing opportunity, and I am so excited to keep on learning at future hackathons! Shoutout to the Cal Hacks team for organizing such an incredible event, Insomnia Cookies for the 2am fuel, and the kind managers at the nearby Hilton hotel who let us crash in their lobby when we couldn't find any available outlets at the Metreon <3

We’ve already identified another attack path in production. More things coming soon.

Two of the biggest breaches of 2026 so far had nothing to do with weak passwords or unpatched CVEs. They operated entirely on credential trust. The Mercor breach (March) started several layers upstream. A threat actor group known as TeamPCP compromised the CI/CD pipeline of LiteLLM, an open-source Python library with 97 million monthly downloads, by first using a supply chain attack on Trivy, a widely used security scanner, to obtain credentials belonging to a LiteLLM maintainer. Those stolen maintainer credentials were used to publish malicious versions of the package. Organizations using lockfiles with poetry.lock or uv.lock were completely protected, but those relying on unpinned or mutable version references inherited the full attack chain. Once you have valid credentials, whether stolen from a CI pipeline or vended by an instance metadata endpoint, the blast radius is determined entirely by what IAM role backs them. The Vercel breach (April) is an even closer analog to the OAuth and credential trust issues that make IAM privilege escalation so dangerous. The attacker inherited a valid OAuth token from a compromised third-party app, and to every system downstream, that token looked completely legitimate. Specifically, a Vercel employee connected a third-party AI tool to their corporate Google account, and attackers used that OAuth connection to take over the employee's Google Workspace account and gain access to Vercel's internal systems, including credentials that were not encrypted. Once inside, the attacker accessed environment variables that weren't marked as sensitive, enumerated them, and used them to expand access further within the environment. A valid token is a valid token, regardless of if it came from a poisoned npm package, a hijacked OAuth app, or an instance metadata endpoint on a port. tldr; the surface changes, the trust model doesn't. I spun up a sandboxed AWS environment to simulate an analogous attack path. Check out my walkthrough!
